lesson.title: Putting a Mean to the Test: The One-Sample T-Test
lesson.summary: A one-sample t-test checks whether a sample mean provides convincing evidence against a claimed population mean, using the t-distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom to judge how unusual the result is.
lesson.body:
A one-sample t-test asks the same basic question as the one-proportion z-test from earlier in this unit, does the sample give convincing evidence against a claimed population value, but for a mean instead of a proportion, and using the t-distribution instead of the normal distribution, since sigma is unknown and must be estimated with s. The hypotheses take the familiar form: H0: mu = mu0, against Ha: mu < mu0, mu > mu0, or mu not equal to mu0. The test statistic is t = (xbar - mu0) / (s / square root of n), with degrees of freedom n - 1.

Suppose a manufacturer claims its batteries last an average of 10 hours. An independent lab tests a random sample of 20 batteries and finds a sample mean life of xbar = 9.6 hours with a sample standard deviation of s = 1.1 hours. Is there convincing evidence, at alpha = 0.05, that the true mean battery life is less than the claimed 10 hours. Set H0: mu = 10 and Ha: mu < 10. The standard error is 1.1 divided by the square root of 20, which is 1.1/4.472 = 0.246. The test statistic is t = (9.6 - 10) / 0.246 = -1.63, with degrees of freedom n - 1 = 19. For a one-sided test at alpha = 0.05 with df = 19, the critical value from a t-table is t* = 1.729. Since the test statistic's magnitude, 1.63, is smaller than the critical value, 1.729, the sample mean is not far enough below 10 to be considered convincing evidence at the 0.05 level, so the lab fails to reject H0.

This does not prove the manufacturer's claim is true, only that this particular sample, with this much variability and this sample size, is not surprising enough under H0 to overturn it. A larger sample, or a sample with less variability in battery life, could easily produce a significant result even with the same underlying gap between 9.6 and 10 hours, which is exactly the power and sample-size logic from the start of this unit. And, as with the t-interval, this conclusion is only as trustworthy as the conditions behind it: the batteries need to have been randomly sampled, the sample needs to represent well under 10 percent of any finite batch being tested, and with n = 20 falling in the moderate range, a quick check of the sample for strong skewness or outliers is warranted before treating this p-value as the final word.
